analysis.one_liner: Tightens court oversight of corporate crime settlements and bans secret no-prosecution deals for corporate offenses.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action; it has 10 Democratic sponsors and no Republican support so far.
analysis.plain_summary: When the Justice Department catches a company breaking federal law, it often lets the company off without a criminal conviction through a deferred prosecution or non-prosecution agreement — a deal to drop or pause the case in exchange for fines and promised reforms. This bill would require a federal judge to approve those deferred deals, bar judges from approving them at all for offenses causing death or serious injury or by repeat offenders, ban paid no-prosecution deals outright, create a dedicated Office of Corporate Enforcement inside the Justice Department, and post the terms of all these agreements — current and past, back to 1993 — on a public website.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of corporate crime, who would get the right to confer with prosecutors before a deal is struck and to be heard by the judge before it is approved, and the general public, which would gain access to the terms of every corporate settlement and an annual accounting of compliance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of corporate crime and the public

how_it_helps.text: Courts could not approve a deferred prosecution agreement unless they find it is in the public interest and its penalties are sufficient to hold the company accountable, compensate victims, and deter repeat offenses [S2].
Victims would have to be able to confer with prosecutors at least 15 days before an agreement is offered and be heard by the court before a judge approves it [S2].

The bill bans the government from entering agreements to decline prosecution of a corporate offense in exchange for money, voiding any such deal, while preserving ordinary plea bargains, immunity deals, and civil consent decrees [S2].
It creates a separate Office of Corporate Enforcement within the Justice Department to monitor compliance with every agreement and report violations to the Deputy Attorney General [S2].

The Attorney General would have to publish the text, terms, fines, and monitor arrangements of deferred and non-prosecution agreements within 30 days, and post agreements dating back to 1993 within three years [S2].
Companies convicted of a similar corporate offense, or that previously entered a similar agreement, could not get another deferred deal — judges could not approve it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations under federal investigation and their executives, who would lose access to quietly negotiated deals, face court oversight of any deferred agreement, and have their settlement terms and prior violations made public; white-collar defense practices built around negotiating such deals would also face new constraints.

drawbacks.text: Requiring court approval of every deferred prosecution agreement could slow or complicate settlements that prosecutors currently use to win compensation and reforms quickly without a trial [S2].

The absolute ban on agreements for offenses involving death or serious injury, or by repeat offenders, removes prosecutorial flexibility — some cases that today end in a monitored settlement would have to be tried or dropped entirely [S2].
The bill leaves the discretion to define what counts as a 'corporate offense' with the Attorney General, so the scope of these new rules depends on whoever holds that office [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades speed and prosecutorial flexibility for accountability: more corporate settlements would face a judge, victims, and public scrutiny, and paid no-prosecution deals would end. The costs are procedural — slower settlements and less room to negotiate — weighed against a system where large companies have generally avoided criminal convictions and their deal terms have not been uniformly public. As a one-party bill with no committee action, the trade-off has not yet been tested on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action so far.

narrative.text: Representative Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill on May 15, 2026, with nine Democratic cosponsors joining her [S2, S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action appears in the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: companies under federal investigation continue to operate under existing practice, since the bill has not advanced beyond its committee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations under federal investigation, so far

for.name: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Corporate Prosecution Reform Act in the House.

for.name: 9 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Norton, Ross, Tlaib, Johnson of Georgia, Evans, Deluzio, and Dean.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral in May 2026 and has not scheduled a markup or any action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, leaving the bill with no bipartisan base in a House where Republicans hold 223 seats.

industries.note: These companies currently can settle federal criminal cases without a conviction through deferred or non-prosecution agreements. The bill would require court approval, ban paid no-prosecution deals, bar repeat offenders from new deferred deals, and publish their settlement terms and prior violations.

A large practice area is built on negotiating these agreements and serving as independent monitors. Court oversight, standardized terms, and mandatory publication would constrain that discretion while creating new work around compliance monitoring and disclosure.
The bill requires disclosure of all monitor arrangements and contemplates monitors filing evidence with courts, formalizing their role in approved agreements.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action since the May referral, and a Republican majority controlling the House floor calendar, the bill is unlikely to receive a markup or a vote before the Congress ends in January 2027; it would need to be reintroduced to continue.
